This type of control is not all-or-nothing: the degree of expression of a gene
depends in a continuous way on the concentration of proteins that regulate it.
This control mechanism is however very noisy: from binding to transcription initiation
to DNA dynamics, everything is constantly jiggling randomly because of thermal motion.
You can think of a gene's expression level as a continuous, but noisy function of TF concentration.
Surprisingly, cell nuclei still manage to control the expression of genes very precisely
using the concentration of transcription factors. Here are two images of a fly
embryo, with the gradient of TF concentration at the top, and below it the expression
level of its cognate gene. To achieve such a sharp gradient, whatever is controlling
this gene's expression must be very sensitive to small differences in concentration

despite being constantly bombarded on all sides by randomly moving molecules,
despite the small differences of concentration which it must distinguish in a short time,
could still exert fine control on gene expression in a biologically and physically plausible way.
I will show you how with generic biological components, making use of fascinating physical
effects, sensitivity to small changes in concentration can be amplified and controlled.

This slope is just the derivative of the average of a log likelihood ratio. We can approximate this
with a quantity commonly used in statistical inference, called the Fisher information rate.
This equivalence is exact in the limit of hard-to-distinguish concentrations. I hope I have
convinced you by now that the larger this quantity is, the more distinguishable concentrations
are, and the faster a decision can be made. In this model, faster binding = faster decisions,
up to the limit allowed by diffusion. Armed with this metric for the quality of decision-
making, we can now quantitatively compare other models of transcription
Up till now, we have used the simplest possible model of transcription initiation, where
mRNA starts being produced as soon as a transcription factor binds to the promoter.
A slightly more realistic model would account for the finite time it takes for this process
to activate and deactivate. We can capture this in the following model with 4 states instead of 2.
You can notice the delay in activating transcription, governed by this rate kon. This has an
interesting effect on the quality of decision making, reflected by the Fisher rate: it decreases
at high c. This means diffusion is no longer the limiting factor, and a receptor would do well
to slow down binding in order to reach maximum sensitivity at high enough c.

the answer depends on concentration: at high concentration, cooperative binding is beneficial

However, we've learned something more interesting: the best promoters don't necessarily
saturate the limits of their performance allowable by general principles. They are always
constrained by physical laws, but those might come up as system-dependent chemical rates.
To me, this says something about using arguments of optimization in biology. Their greatest
value is not to make quantitative predictions from optimality principles, but to force us to
confront the rich behavior arising from the real physical constraints biological systems
are subject to. This diversity may be biologically informative and interesting in its own right.

Let's now step back and take a better look at how biology actually carries out transcription.
So far we've been assuming that the promoter is the only control mechanism responsible
for launching RNA Polymerase and transcribing a gene. In eukaryotes, which include all
organisms except bacteria and archaea, distant parts of DNA are known to play a central
role in transcription initiation. Like promoters, these are non-coding sequences, known as
enhancers. However, they can be hundreds of thousands of base pairs away from a gene.
How these sequences can benefit precise gene regulation despite being so far away
has been a puzzle in biology for many years.
promoter
gene

Another ingredient has been emergencing in this recipe, building on recent experimental evidence:
surface condensation. I've told you that transcription factors may bind cooperatively on the
promoter, and that benefits the decision problem at high concentration. What has been shown
to happen, with many different molecules, is condensation of a liquid-like droplet on the
surface of DNA. this is a physical phenomenon that has been studied since the 1970s, called
pre-wetting. It is the formation of a dense phase of a liquid around an area that attracts
species that is otherwise diluted in the bulk, and importantly, below the concentration at which
it saturates.

We wondered what a gene regulation mechanism that accounts for this biological reality
would look like. I started by building intuition with lattice simulations of polymers
in 3D space interacting with dilute molecules, representing regulatory proteins.
Here the orange segment of DNA represents a promoter near the gene, and the red
segment is a distant enhancer. blue particle attach to both orange and red, and to each
other. The black dot here is the place where RNA polymerase binds and launches
transcription. Blue particles represent regulatory molecules, both TF and RNA Pol.
Transcription initiates whenever a blue particle attaches to the black dot.
You can see that because blue particles condense on the regulatory regions,
and because they are attracted to each other, they act like glue. This glue acts at very short
range, it cannot bring distant parts of DNA together. However, when they do happen to come
in contact, it keeps them close together much longer than they would otherwise.

This is very promising, because it could give us a way to make transcription depend
sensitively on concentration. So let's try to understand what exactly is going on here.
Like good physicists, suppose we model a promoter as a sphere. The standard way to
describe mixtures of liquids at equilibrium is Flory-Huggins theory. If we are dealing with
just a mixture of two fluids, this theory predicts the temperature and concentrations at
which they form separate phases, like oil and water, and when they are homogeneously
mixed. Adding an attractive surface can create a local phase separation while the rest
of the mixture is homogeneous. This is the phenomenon we're interested in, because it
turns out to be very sensitive to concentration, as these plots show. Here is local
concentration at the surface, as a function of concentration of a protein in the mixture.
Here is how it depends on the radius of the sphere, and here dependence on how strongly
it attracts transcription factors.

We can also compute the Fisher information rate gain from this nonlinear dependence of
local concentration on background concentration, highlighted by the term in read.
A single promoter can produce a strong peak in Fisher rate. This means that in principle, the
effect of condensation on its own would be sufficient to explain high concentration sensitivity.
Condensation is a double-edged sword, however, because outside the range of amplification
it actually reduces sensitivity. If the sphere is attractive enough, it can even dampen the
signal across all concentrations, which is unproductive.
However something more interesting goes on when we think about the distal enhancer.
When two attractive surfaces come together, they form a capillary bridge. The formation of
this bridge is also very sensitive to concentration. So we solved the Cahn-Hilliard equation
with two spheres, and from there we could compute exactly the potential and the force
that arise from this capillary bridge, and crucially, their dependence on concentration.

But what about the rest of the polymer? The promoter and enhancer are tethered together
on the same piece of DNA. We chose to model this with a Rouse polymer, since it is analytically
tractable: we have an equation that describes the equilibrium separation between the beads.
Rouse polymer parameters
expression for steady-state potential
We can now combine these two potentials together, and this captures both the effect of the
polymer and of the short-range capillary force on the position of the two beads. It also
gives us an equation of motion, the Langevin equation, that lets us simulate this polymer
and study its dynamics. From there, we can compute the distributions of time the polymer
spends open and closed. The dynamics of a Rouse polymer usually is not Markovian,
however we assumed that these opening and closing durations were independent.
This lets us compute the likelihood of a trajectory, and therefore, the Fisher information.
closed and open time PDFs
One thing I'll tell you so that you appreciate this result. Remember how we found that the
Fisher information of a single receptor was equal to the rate of turning on and off?
That is, the inverse of the average duration of an ON/OFF cycle. In our model, we choose
our diffusion coefficient D, which sets the timescale of the polymer simulation, such that
the closing and opening times of a polymer were much larger than the burst time of a single
receptor. Still, comparing the Fisher information rates in the same units, we found that the
polymer can still give you more sensitivity, per unit time, than a single receptor. This is
true even if it takes the polymer over 100 times longer to produce a single "burst"

The value of thinking in terms of optimization forces us, physicists, to confront
hard constraints imposed by real biology. These constraints are what set
the physical scales of solutions to biological problems, and determine the shapes they take.
We learn interesting things by confronting the fact that optimal solutions depend
intimately on the constraints they saturate, this sheds light on biologically meaningful
tradeoffs that evolution is subject to.
There is no reason to believe that evolution optimizes individual components
independently of each other. A more realistic take is that the promoter's environment
plays an active role in the sensing process
